::: {.callout-note title="Historical model and clean rerun"}
This summary describes the original 350-round model and its Kaggle submission.
A clean run with explicit seed 6812 selected a 525-round model at 0.78265 mean
five-fold AUC. That new fit has not been scored on Kaggle. See
[REPRODUCIBILITY.md](REPRODUCIBILITY.md) for the clean-run record.
:::

## Recommendation

**Keep the current XGBoost model as the project's research model.** It was the
best performer among the models tested on the same data and validation folds.
Its score on Kaggle's hidden test applicants was close to its cross-validation
score, which gives additional evidence that it can rank new applicants by risk.
It is suitable for analysis and a controlled review process, but further work is
needed before it could support real lending decisions.

## What the model does

The model gives each loan application a score for the chance of **payment
difficulty** (`TARGET = 1`). A higher score means the applicant is ranked as
more likely to have difficulty. The score is a way to prioritize review; it is
not an automatic approve-or-decline decision. The competition outcome is
payment difficulty, which is not necessarily the same as a loan charge-off or
financial loss.

The model learned from **307,511 labeled applications**. It uses the current
application plus summarized information from six Home Credit history tables:
`bureau`, `bureau_balance`, `previous_application`, `installments_payments`,
`POS_CASH_balance`, and `credit_card_balance`. This gives it more information
about past borrowing and repayment behavior than an application-only model.
About **8.07%** of the labeled applications have the payment-difficulty outcome,
so simply calling everyone low risk would appear accurate while doing little to
identify higher-risk applicants.

## Evidence for selecting XGBoost

All candidates in this project were evaluated on the **same five stratified
cross-validation folds**. In each fold, preparation steps that learn from data
were fitted on the training portion and then applied to the held-out portion.
This makes the model comparison more dependable.

| Model tested in this project | Mean cross-validated ROC AUC |
|---|---:|
| Constant-score baseline | 0.5000 |
| Pruned decision tree | 0.6528 |
| Random forest | 0.7504 |
| Elastic-net logistic regression | 0.7629 |
| **Selected XGBoost** | **0.7825** |

*ROC AUC* measures how well a model places applicants with payment difficulty
above applicants without it. A score of 0.50 is no better than random ranking;
higher is better. XGBoost exceeded the next-best model, elastic-net logistic
regression, by **0.0196 AUC** on these folds. Its fold-to-fold standard deviation
was **0.0018**. This is evidence for choosing XGBoost **within the set of models
tested here**; it does not prove that no other algorithm could do better.

The final model uses **350 boosting rounds**, trees with a maximum depth of
**7**, and a learning rate of **0.05**. It lets XGBoost use missing values
directly. In the project experiments, that worked better than filling every
numeric gap with a median. Adding class weights reduced ranking performance and
worsened probability error. Increasing the leading configuration from 350 to
525 rounds did not improve validation performance, so the 350-round version was
retained.

## Check on applicants outside model selection

After selection, the model was refitted on all labeled applications and scored
Kaggle's separate test applicants, whose outcomes were hidden from the project:

| Evaluation | ROC AUC |
|---|---:|
| Five-fold cross-validation mean | 0.7825 |
| Kaggle public test subset | 0.78617 |
| **Kaggle private test subset** | **0.77982** |

The private score is only **about 0.003** below the cross-validation mean. The
similar scores support the conclusion that the validation result was a useful
estimate for this competition. They do not measure performance on today's loan
applicants or in a live lending process.

### Context from the three linked projects

The linked READMEs also report XGBoost as their selected model. Their Kaggle
private scores provide a common competition reference, though each project uses
different features and validation steps. The figures below are the projects'
reported results; they were not reproduced for this summary.

| Project | History tables used for its selected model | Reported Kaggle private ROC AUC |
|---|---|---:|
| [Silva](https://github.com/aadssilva/home-credit-project/blob/main/README.md) | None; application only | 0.74116 |
| [Jackson](https://github.com/bradynjackson/home-credit-default-risk/blob/main/README.md) | None; application only | 0.75817 |
| [Hoopes](https://github.com/HoopesJake11/home-credit-project/blob/main/README.md) | `bureau` | 0.75276 |
| **Current project** | Six history tables listed above | **0.77982** |

The current project has the highest reported private score in this group. The
comparison does **not** show how much of the difference comes from the extra
tables, feature engineering, or model settings.

## What still needs review

- **Probability accuracy:** ROC AUC measures ranking, not whether a predicted
  risk such as 10% will correspond to a 10% event rate in future applicants.
  The project has an out-of-fold calibration check, but future-population
  calibration remains unverified.
- **Fairness and explanations:** The model uses demographic fields and external
  scores whose construction is not documented in the competition data. Group
  outcomes, feature use, and applicant-specific explanations need further review.
- **Business value:** The dataset does not provide the actual pricing, funding
  costs, or realized loan losses needed to verify a profit-maximizing approval
  threshold. Financial examples in the model card are scenarios, not measured
  returns.
- **Transfer to real lending:** The historical competition applicants may differ
  from current applicants. Results on rejected applicants cannot be measured
  directly from these data.

**Selection decision:** Use this XGBoost model as the strongest **tested research
benchmark** for risk ranking. Before considering operational use, compare any
new candidate on the same folds and features, validate probabilities and group
outcomes on a representative population, and review whether the model's inputs
and explanations are appropriate for lending decisions.
